clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer a hazardous antineoplastic drug for which a protective gown is indicated. Which gown is the most appropriate choice?

options.A: A disposable laminate barrier gown with long sleeves and tight-fitting cuffs.
options.B: An absorbent cloth laboratory coat with long sleeves and loose cuffs.
options.C: A short-sleeved isolation gown worn with chemotherapy gloves over the hands.
options.D: A previously worn hazardous-drug gown that is dry and has no visible contamination.

semantic_correction.rationale: OSHA hazardous-drug guidance states that protective gowns should not have seams or closures that allow drug passage and should have long sleeves with tight-fitting cuffs. Disposable polyethylene-coated polypropylene or other laminate materials offer better protection than non-coated absorbent materials, while cloth laboratory coats and scrubs can absorb hazardous drugs. OSHA also advises disposing of gowns after each use because reuse increases exposure risk. Therefore, option A best matches the recommended protective-gown characteristics.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Select a hazardous-drug protective gown that provides a nonabsorbent barrier with long sleeves and tight-fitting cuffs, and do not reuse previously worn gowns.
semantic_correction.source_organization: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: shortened the correct answer, rebuilt all distractors as realistic gown choices, and avoided claiming that a single 'chemotherapy-tested' gown performance label is universally required because OSHA notes no single specific performance standard for gown permeation.

audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed pp. 24–25
audit_findings_append.finding: The original correct answer was uniquely longest. The revised item tests the core gown characteristics with concise, parallel choices and preserves OSHA's nuance that there is no single specific chemotherapy-gown performance standard.

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches the recommended barrier material, sleeve length, and cuff design.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. OSHA notes that absorbent cloth materials permit hazardous-drug penetration and can hold spilled drug against the skin.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Short sleeves do not provide the recommended long-sleeve forearm barrier even when gloves are used.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. OSHA advises disposal after each use because reuse increases the likelihood of hazardous-drug exposure.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone combines the OSHA-recommended barrier material, sleeve/cuff design, and single-use approach among the choices.
cueing_check: All four choices are gown-selection descriptions of comparable length and detail; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
